q: A solutions architect needs to allow team members to access Amazon S3 buckets in two different AWS accounts: a development account and a production account. The team currently has access to S3 buckets in the development account by using unique IAM users that are assigned to an IAM group that has appropriate permissions in the account. The solutions architect has created an IAM role in the production account. The role has a policy that grants access to an S3 bucket in the production account. Which solution will meet these requirements while complying with the principle of least privilege?

o.t: Create a user in the production account with unique credentials for each team member.
o.w: Creating per-user IAM accounts in production duplicates identity management across accounts and does not use the cross-account role already built, adding unnecessary standing credentials.

o.t: Turn off the S3 Block Public Access feature on the S3 bucket in the production account.
o.w: Disabling S3 Block Public Access would expose the bucket to the entire internet, which is the opposite of least privilege and unrelated to cross-account access.

o.t: Add the development account as a principal in the trust policy of the role in the production account.
o.w: Adding the development account as a trusted principal lets its IAM users assume the production role via STS and receive only the temporary, scoped permissions the role's policy grants.

o.t: Attach the Administrator Access policy to the development account users.
o.w: Attaching AdministratorAccess to development users grants far more permissions than needed to read one S3 bucket, violating least privilege.

explain:
By adding the development account as a principal in the trust policy of the IAM role in the production account, you enable IAM users in the development account to assume the role and gain temporary permissions to access the S3 bucket in the production account.

This approach follows the principle of least privilege because it allows users in the development account to access only the specific resources (S3 bucket) defined in the trust policy of the IAM role.

q: A company hosts a serverless application on AWS. The application uses Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database. The company notices an increase in application errors that result from database connection timeouts during times of peak traffic or unpredictable traffic. The company needs a solution that reduces the application failures with the least amount of change to the code. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

o.t: Resize the RDS DB instance class to accept more connections.
o.w: Resizing the instance class adds more connection headroom but doesn't fix the root cause of unmanaged, bursty connection churn from Lambda, and requires ongoing capacity changes as traffic grows.

o.t: Enable RDS Proxy on the RDS DB instance.
o.w: RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes database connections so that bursts of concurrent Lambda invocations don't each open a new connection, preventing connection exhaustion with no application code changes.

o.t: Reduce the Lambda concurrency rate.
o.w: Reducing Lambda concurrency limits how many requests can be served at once, which would make timeouts and errors worse during peak traffic, not better.

o.t: Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand scaling.
o.w: Migrating to DynamoDB would require substantial code and data-model changes, failing the 'least amount of change' requirement.

explain: RDS Proxy is a fully managed, highly available database proxy that can handle database connections for serverless and highly scalable applications. It helps manage database connections efficiently, reducing issues related to connection timeouts and errors.

q: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer that has sticky sessions enabled. The web server currently hosts the user session state. The company wants to ensure high availability and avoid user session state loss in the event of a web server outage. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Use an AWS Storage Gateway cached volume to store session data. Update the application to use AWS Storage Gateway cached volume to store the session state.
o.w: Storage Gateway is designed for hybrid on-premises file and block storage integration with S3, not for storing fast-changing web session state.

o.t: Use Amazon RDS to store the session state. Update the application to use Amazon RDS to store the session state.
o.w: RDS is a relational database; using it for ephemeral session data adds unnecessary schema and connection overhead and higher latency than an in-memory store.

o.t: Use an Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached instance to store the session data. Update the application to use ElastiCache for Memcached to store the session state.
o.w: Memcached does not natively support replication or multi-AZ failover, so a node failure would still cause session data loss.

o.t: Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to store the session state. Update the application to use ElastiCache for Redis to store the session state.
o.w: ElastiCache for Redis supports multi-AZ replication with automatic failover, so session state persists and stays available even if an individual cache node or web server fails.

explain: ElastiCache for Redis is an in-memory data store service that is well-suited for storing session data. It provides high availability and durability. Using Redis allows the application to offload the session state from individual EC2 instances to a centralized and highly available Redis cluster.

q: A retail company has several businesses. The IT team for each business manages its own AWS account. Each team account is part of an organization in AWS Organizations. Each team monitors its product inventory levels in an Amazon DynamoDB table in the team's own AWS account. The company is deploying a central inventory reporting application into a shared AWS account. The application must be able to read items from all the teams' DynamoDB tables. Which authentication option will meet these requirements MOST securely?

o.t: Integrate DynamoDB with AWS Secrets Manager in the inventory application account. Configure the application to use the correct secret from Secrets Manager to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table. Schedule secret rotation for every 30 days.
o.w: A static secret in Secrets Manager is a long-lived credential that still must be distributed and rotated manually, which is less secure than temporary STS credentials obtained through role assumption.

o.t: Integrate DynamoDB with AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Generate identity certificates to authenticate DynamoDB. Configure the application to use the correct certificate to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table.
o.w: ACM issues TLS certificates for encrypting traffic; it is not an identity or authentication mechanism for granting AWS API access to DynamoDB, so it cannot satisfy this requirement.

o.t: In every business account, create an IAM user that has programmatic access. Configure the application to use the correct IAM user access key ID and secret access key to authenticate and read the DynamoDB table. Manually rotate IAM access keys every 30 days.
o.w: Long-lived IAM user access keys in every account must be distributed and manually rotated, creating standing credentials that increase the blast radius if leaked, the opposite of 'most securely.'

o.t: In every business account, create an IAM role named BU_ROLE with a policy that gives the role access to the DynamoDB table and a trust policy to trust a specific role in the inventory application account. In the inventory account, create a role named APP_ROLE that allows access to the STS AssumeRole API operation. Configure the application to use APP_ROLE and assume the crossaccount role BU_ROLE to read the DynamoDB table.
o.w: Having the inventory app assume a per-business IAM role via STS grants only temporary, scoped credentials restricted to each team's DynamoDB table, with no long-lived keys to manage.

q: A company has 700 TB of backup data stored in network attached storage (NAS) in its data center. This backup data need to be accessible for infrequent regulatory requests and must be retained 7 years. The company has decided to migrate this backup data from its data center to AWS. The migration must be complete within 1 month. The company has 500 Mbps of dedicated bandwidth on its public internet connection available for data transfer. What should a solutions architect do to migrate and store the data at the LOWEST cost?

o.t: Deploy a VPN connection between the data center and Amazon VPC. Use the AWS CLI to copy the data from on premises to Amazon S3 Glacier.
o.w: VPN over the public internet at 500 Mbps would take far longer than a month to move 700 TB, and S3 Glacier is not a direct CLI upload target, so data would still need to land in S3 first.

o.t: Provision a 500 Mbps AWS Direct Connect connection and transfer the data to Amazon S3. Use a lifecycle policy to transition the files to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
o.w: Provisioning Direct Connect for a one-time transfer takes weeks to arrange and carries recurring connection fees, making it slower to set up and costlier than a one-time Snowball shipment for archival data.

o.t: Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data and deploy a DataSync agent on premises. Use the DataSync task to copy files from the on-premises NAS storage to Amazon S3 Glacier.
o.w: At 500 Mbps, transferring 700 TB over the internet via DataSync would take many months, far exceeding the one-month deadline, and S3 Glacier is not a direct DataSync destination.

o.t: Order AWS Snowball devices to transfer the data. Use a lifecycle policy to transition the files to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
o.w: Snowball physically ships the data to AWS in days regardless of internet bandwidth, meeting the one-month deadline, and a lifecycle policy to Glacier Deep Archive gives the lowest-cost storage for data accessed only infrequently over 7 years.

explain:
AWS Snowball: AWS Snowball is a physical data transfer service that allows you to securely transfer large amounts of data into and out of AWS. In this scenario, with 700 TB of data, using Snowball devices can expedite the transfer process. It's a one-time cost-efficient solution for large data transfers.
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive: After transferring the data to Amazon S3 using Snowball, you can use a lifecycle policy to transition the files to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive. This storage class is designed for infrequently accessed data with a retention requirement of 7 years, aligning with the regulatory compliance needs.

q: A company serves a dynamic website from a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The website needs to support multiple languages to serve customers around the world. The website’s architecture is running in the us-west-1 Region and is exhibiting high request latency for users that are located in other parts of the world. The website needs to serve requests quickly and efficiently regardless of a user’s location. However, the company does not want to recreate the existing architecture across multiple Regions. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

o.t: Launch an EC2 instance in each additional Region and configure NGINX to act as a cache server for that Region. Put all the EC2 instances and the ALB behind an Amazon Route 53 record set with a geolocation routing policy.
o.w: Running custom NGINX cache servers in every Region requires building and maintaining infrastructure in multiple Regions, which the company explicitly wants to avoid, and is far more complex than a managed CDN.

o.t: Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the ALB as the origin. Set the cache behavior settings to cache based on the AcceptLanguage request header.
o.w: CloudFront caches content at edge locations close to users worldwide and can vary cached objects by the Accept-Language header, serving localized content with low latency without duplicating the origin architecture.

o.t: Replace the existing architecture with a website that is served from an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as the origin. Set the cache behavior settings to cache based on the Accept-Language request header.
o.w: Replacing the EC2/ALB architecture with a static S3-hosted site would require rebuilding the dynamic application, which isn't feasible since the site is dynamic, not static content.

o.t: Create an Amazon API Gateway API that is integrated with the ALB. Configure the API to use the HTTP integration type. Set up an API Gateway stage to enable the API cache based on the Accept-Language request header.
o.w: API Gateway's cache is keyed for API responses, not full web pages, adding an extra hop without providing global edge caching comparable to a CDN, and traffic still routes back to us-west-1.

q: A company provides an API interface to customers so the customers can retrieve their financial information. Еhe company expects a larger number of requests during peak usage times of the year. The company requires the API to respond consistently with low latency to ensure customer satisfaction. The company needs to provide a compute host for the API. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

o.t: Use Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda functions with reserved concurrency.
o.w: Reserved concurrency alone guarantees a ceiling but doesn't pre-initialize execution environments, so cold starts can still introduce latency spikes during sudden peak traffic.

o.t: Use an Application Load Balancer and Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS).
o.w: ALB plus ECS requires managing container task scaling and cluster capacity, which is more operational overhead than a fully serverless option.

o.t: Use an Application Load Balancer and an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster.
o.w: ALB plus EKS requires standing up and operating a Kubernetes control plane and worker nodes, the highest operational overhead of the choices.

o.t: Use Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda functions with provisioned concurrency.
o.w: API Gateway with Lambda provisioned concurrency keeps execution environments warm and ready, giving consistent low-latency responses during peak usage while remaining fully serverless with minimal management.

explain:
Amazon API Gateway is a fully managed service that makes it easy for developers to create, publish, maintain, monitor, and secure APIs at any scale.
AWS Lambda is a serverless computing service that automatically scales based on demand.
Provisioned concurrency in AWS Lambda allows you to set a specific number of concurrent executions to ensure that the function is ready to respond quickly to incoming requests.

q: A company wants to migrate an Oracle database to AWS. The database consists of a single table that contains millions of geographic information systems (GIS) images that are high resolution and are identified by a geographic code. When a natural disaster occurs, tens of thousands of images get updated every few minutes. Each geographic code has a single image or row that is associated with it. The company wants a solution that is highly available and scalable during such events. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Store the images and geographic codes in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Configure DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) during times of high load.
o.w: DynamoDB alone would need to store large high-resolution images as item attributes, which is inefficient and costly compared to object storage, even with DAX for read caching.

o.t: Store the images and geographic codes in a database table. Use Oracle running on an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.
o.w: Keeping Oracle on RDS for both images and metadata means storing large binary images in a relational database, which is costly and scales less efficiently for bursty, write-heavy image updates than a dedicated object store.

o.t: Store the images in Amazon S3 buckets. Use Amazon DynamoDB with the geographic code as the key and the image S3 URL as the value.
o.w: Using DynamoDB for geographic codes without a relational engine loses the ability to run structured relational queries and still doesn't leverage the existing Oracle-compatible tooling, making it a less complete, cost-effective fit than keeping a relational metadata table alongside S3.

o.t: Store the images in Amazon S3 buckets. Store geographic codes and image S3 URLs in a database table. Use Oracle running on an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance.
o.w: Storing images in S3 avoids expensive database storage for large binaries, while a Multi-AZ Oracle RDS table holding just codes and URLs remains available and durable, giving a cost-effective, highly available design for the burst update pattern.

explain: Explanation: Each geographic code maps to a single image/row — a simple key-value access pattern — and updates arrive in spiky bursts during disasters. DynamoDB is built for exactly that: high, unpredictable write throughput with simple key lookups, scaling more cost-effectively than a relational Oracle-on-RDS table for this access pattern.

q: A company hosts an application on Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances in an Auto Scaling group. Application peak hours occur at the same time each day. Application users report slow application performance at the start of peak hours. The application performs normally 2-3 hours after peak hours begin. The company wants to ensure that the application works properly at the start of peak hours. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Configure a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on memory utilization.
o.w: Dynamic scaling based on memory still reacts only after the metric threshold is breached, so it won't pre-provision capacity before peak hours begin and the slow start persists.

o.t: Configure a scheduled scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances before peak hours.
o.w: Scheduled scaling launches additional instances ahead of the known, predictable peak time each day, so capacity is already in place when peak traffic starts.

o.t: Configure an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic properly to the instances.
o.w: An ALB only distributes traffic across existing instances; it doesn't add capacity, so it won't fix a shortage of running instances at the start of peak hours.

o.t: Configure a dynamic scaling policy for the Auto Scaling group to launch new instances based on CPU utilization.
o.w: Dynamic scaling based on CPU utilization, like the memory-based option, only scales out after utilization rises, so there is still a lag at the very start of each day's predictable peak.

q: A company runs an online marketplace web application on AWS. The application serves hundreds of thousands of users during peak hours. The company needs a scalable, near-real-time solution to share the details of millions of financial transactions with several other internal applications. Transactions also need to be processed to remove sensitive data before being stored in a document database for low-latency retrieval. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

o.t: Stream the transactions data into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Use AWS Lambda integration to remove sensitive data from every transaction and then store the transactions data in Amazon DynamoDB. Other applications can consume the transactions data off the Kinesis data stream.
o.w: Kinesis Data Streams ingests transactions in near real time at scale, Lambda can process each record to strip sensitive data before writing to DynamoDB for low-latency lookups, and other applications can independently consume the same stream.

o.t: Store the transactions data into Amazon DynamoDB. Set up a rule in DynamoDB to remove sensitive data from every transaction upon write. Use DynamoDB Streams to share the transactions data with other applications.
o.w: DynamoDB has no native rule engine to redact data on write, so this isn't a real capability, and DynamoDB Streams alone doesn't provide the same ordered, multi-consumer, near-real-time fan-out that Kinesis offers for sharing with many downstream apps.

o.t: Store the batched transactions data in Amazon S3 as files. Use AWS Lambda to process every file and remove sensitive data before updating the files in Amazon S3. The Lambda function then stores the data in Amazon DynamoDB. Other applications can consume transaction files stored in Amazon S3.
o.w: Batching transactions into S3 files introduces delay that breaks the near-real-time requirement, and processing whole files for every update is less efficient than streaming individual records.

o.t: Stream the transactions data into Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to store data in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3. Use AWS Lambda integration with Kinesis Data Firehose to remove sensitive data. Other applications can consume the data stored in Amazon S3.
o.w: Kinesis Data Firehose buffers data for seconds to minutes and is best suited for loading data into storage like S3, not as a true low-latency stream for multiple independently consuming applications.

explain:
1. Real-time Data Stream: To share millions of financial transactions with other apps, you need to be able to ingest data in real-time, which is made possible by Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.

2. Data Transformation: You can cleanse and eliminate sensitive data from transactions before storing them in Amazon DynamoDB by utilizing AWS Lambda with Kinesis Data Streams. This takes care of the requirement to handle sensitive data with care.
3. Scalability: DynamoDB and Amazon Kinesis are both extremely scalable technologies that can manage enormous data volumes and adjust to the workload.

q: A company's applications run on Amazon EC2 instances in Auto Scaling groups. The company notices that its applications experience sudden traffic increases on random days of the week. The company wants to maintain application performance during sudden traffic increases. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Use dynamic scaling to change the size of the Auto Scaling group.
o.w: Dynamic scaling reacts to real-time demand automatically, scaling out only when traffic actually spikes and back in when it subsides, handling unpredictable spikes without paying for idle capacity on non-spike days.

o.t: Use predictive scaling to change the size of the Auto Scaling group.
o.w: Predictive scaling relies on historical patterns to forecast capacity ahead of time; since the spikes occur on random, unpredictable days, forecasting provides little benefit and risks over- or under-provisioning.

o.t: Use manual scaling to change the size of the Auto Scaling group.
o.w: Manual scaling requires a person to adjust capacity, which cannot react in time to sudden, unplanned traffic increases and adds operational burden.

o.t: Use schedule scaling to change the size of the Auto Scaling group.
o.w: Scheduled scaling only adjusts capacity at fixed, known times, which doesn't help when spikes occur on random, unpredictable days.

explain: Dynamic Scaling: With dynamic scaling, the Auto Scaling group automatically adjusts its capacity based on real-time demand. It scales out during traffic spikes and scales in during periods of lower demand. This ensures that your application can handle sudden increases in traffic without manual intervention.

q: A company that uses AWS is building an application to transfer data to a product manufacturer. The company has its own identity provider (IdP). The company wants the IdP to authenticate application users while the users use the application to transfer data. The company must use Applicability Statement 2 (AS2) protocol. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Use AWS Transfer Family to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.
o.w: AWS Transfer Family natively supports the AS2 protocol for file transfer, and it supports custom identity providers via an AWS Lambda function for authentication, meeting both requirements directly.

o.t: Use Amazon AppFlow flows to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task for IdP authentication.
o.w: Amazon AppFlow integrates SaaS applications with AWS services via APIs; it does not support the AS2 file transfer protocol.

o.t: Use AWS Storage Gateway to transfer the data. Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool for IdP authentication.
o.w: AWS Storage Gateway provides file, volume, and tape gateways for hybrid storage; it does not support the AS2 protocol for transferring data to a partner.

o.t: Use AWS DataSync to transfer the data. Create an AWS Lambda function for IdP authentication.
o.w: AWS DataSync is built for moving files between on-premises storage and AWS storage services; it does not support the AS2 protocol used for this B2B data exchange.

explain: AWS Transfer Family (Option C): AWS Transfer Family is a fully managed service that allows you to transfer files over the internet using a range of protocols, including AS2. You can integrate AWS Transfer Family with your IdP for user authentication. By using a Lambda function, you can customize the authentication process and integrate it with your own IdP.

q: A company hosts its multi-tier applications on AWS. For compliance, governance, auditing, and security, the company must track configuration changes on its AWS resources and record a history of API calls made to these resources. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

o.t: Use AWS CloudTrail to track configuration changes and AWS Config to record API calls.
o.w: This reverses the services' purposes: CloudTrail logs API calls, not configuration change history, and Config, not CloudWatch, records configuration changes.

o.t: Use AWS CloudTrail to track configuration changes and Amazon CloudWatch to record API calls.
o.w: CloudWatch is a monitoring and logging service, not a service that records the history of API calls; that is CloudTrail's job, and this option still misassigns CloudTrail to configuration tracking.

o.t: Use AWS Config to track configuration changes and Amazon CloudWatch to record API calls.
o.w: CloudWatch does not record API call history; that is the role of CloudTrail, so this combination doesn't meet the API-call-tracking requirement.

o.t: Use AWS Config to track configuration changes and AWS CloudTrail to record API calls.
o.w: AWS Config continuously tracks and records how resource configurations change over time, while AWS CloudTrail logs every API call made against AWS resources, together satisfying both the configuration-history and API-audit requirements.

explain:
AWS Config for Configuration Changes: AWS Config is a service that tracks changes to resource configurations over time. It provides a history of configuration changes to your AWS resources and helps with compliance and auditing by allowing you to assess how resource configurations have changed over time.

AWS CloudTrail for API Calls: AWS CloudTrail is designed specifically for recording API calls made to AWS resources. It captures detailed information about who made each API call, the actions taken, and the resources affected. This is essential for auditing and security purposes.

q: A company manages an application that stores data on an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Increases in traffic are causing performance problems. The company determines that database queries are the primary reason for the slow performance. What should a solutions architect do to improve the application's performance?

o.t: Configure the DB instance to use Transfer Acceleration.
o.w: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads to Amazon S3 over long distances; it has nothing to do with RDS query performance.

o.t: Serve read traffic from the Multi-AZ standby replica.
o.w: The Multi-AZ standby replica is for failover only and is not available to serve live read traffic in standard RDS Multi-AZ (non-Aurora) deployments.

o.t: Create a read replica from the source DB instance. Serve read traffic from the read replica.
o.w: A read replica offloads read-only query traffic from the primary instance, letting read-heavy workloads scale separately and relieving the pressure that was causing slow performance.

o.t: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose between the application and Amazon RDS to increase the concurrency of database requests.
o.w: Kinesis Data Firehose is a data-delivery service for streaming data into destinations like S3; it does not sit between an application and RDS to increase query concurrency.

explain: Creating read replicas allows you to offload read traffic from the primary (master) DB instance to one or more read replicas. Read replicas can serve read-only queries, distributing the load and improving overall query performance.

q: A company runs an ecommerce application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones. The Auto Scaling group scales based on CPU utilization metrics. The ecommerce application stores the transaction data in a MySQL 8.0 database that is hosted on a large EC2 instance. The database's performance degrades quickly as application load increases. The application handles more read requests than write transactions. The company wants a solution that will automatically scale the database to meet the demand of unpredictable read workloads while maintaining high availability. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Use Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with EC2 Spot Instances.
o.w: ElastiCache for Memcached with Spot Instances would require re-architecting the app to use a cache layer, and Spot Instances can be reclaimed at any time, undermining the high-availability requirement.

o.t: Use Amazon RDS with a Single-AZ deployment Configure Amazon RDS to add reader instances in a different Availability Zone.
o.w: Single-AZ RDS does not provide high availability, and standard RDS read replicas (not Aurora) do not auto-scale automatically in response to load the way Aurora Auto Scaling does.

o.t: Use Amazon Redshift with a single node for leader and compute functionality.
o.w: Redshift is a data warehouse optimized for analytical OLAP queries, not a transactional, high-availability OLTP replacement for a MySQL transactional database.

o.t: Use Amazon Aurora with a Multi-AZ deployment. Configure Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas.
o.w: Aurora Multi-AZ provides high availability through automatic failover, and Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas automatically adds or removes read replicas to match unpredictable read demand.

explain:
Option C: Using Amazon Aurora with a Multi-AZ deployment and configuring Aurora Auto Scaling with Aurora Replicas is the most appropriate solution. Aurora is a MySQL-compatible relational database engine that provides high performance and scalability. With Multi-AZ deployment, the database is automatically replicated across multiple Availability Zones for high availability.
Aurora Auto Scaling allows the database to automatically add or remove Aurora Replicas based on the workload, ensuring that read requests can be distributed effectively and the database can scale to meet demand. This provides both high availability and automatic scaling to handle unpredictable read workloads.

q: A company has an on-premises application that generates a large amount of time-sensitive data that is backed up to Amazon S3. The application has grown and there are user complaints about internet bandwidth limitations. A solutions architect needs to design a long-term solution that allows for both timely backups to Amazon S3 and with minimal impact on internet connectivity for internal users. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Submit a support ticket through the AWS Management Console. Request the removal of S3 service limits from the account.
o.w: S3 service limits are not the bottleneck here; the constraint is internet bandwidth, and a support ticket would not meaningfully change that.

o.t: Establish a new AWS Direct Connect connection and direct backup traffic through this new connection.
o.w: Direct Connect provides a dedicated network connection from the data center to AWS that is separate from the shared internet connection used by internal users, allowing timely backups without consuming bandwidth they need.

o.t: Establish AWS VPN connections and proxy all traffic through a VPC gateway endpoint.
o.w: A VPN still runs over the public internet connection, competing with the same bandwidth that internal users need, so it does not relieve the bandwidth contention problem.

o.t: Order daily AWS Snowball devices. Load the data onto the Snowball devices and return the devices to AWS each day.
o.w: Shipping Snowball devices daily is impractical and costly for an ongoing, time-sensitive backup need; Snowball is suited for large one-time or periodic bulk transfers, not continuous daily backups.

explain: AWS Direct Connect is a network service that allows you to establish a dedicated network connection from your on-premises data center to AWS. This connection bypasses the public Internet and can provide more reliable, lower-latency communication between your on-premises application and Amazon S3. By directing backup traffic through the AWS Direct Connect connection, you can minimize the impact on your internet bandwidth and ensure timely backups to S3.

q: A development team runs monthly resource-intensive tests on its general purpose Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with Performance Insights enabled. The testing lasts for 48 hours once a month and is the only process that uses the database. The team wants to reduce the cost of running the tests without reducing the compute and memory attributes of the DB instance. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Use an Auto Scaling policy with the DB instance to automatically scale when tests are completed.
o.w: RDS does not support an 'Auto Scaling policy' that automatically resizes an instance the way EC2 Auto Scaling does; this isn't a real mechanism for this use case.

o.t: Modify the DB instance to a low-capacity instance when tests are completed. Modify the DB instance again when required.
o.w: Resizing the DB instance to a smaller class to cut costs, then resizing it back up, would reduce the compute and memory attributes, which violates the requirement not to reduce them.

o.t: Stop the DB instance when tests are completed. Restart the DB instance when required.
o.w: A stopped RDS instance still incurs storage costs and can typically remain stopped for only a limited number of days before AWS automatically restarts it, making it a poor fit for a monthly, once-a-month 48-hour cycle.

o.t: Create a snapshot when tests are completed. Terminate the DB instance and restore the snapshot when required.
o.w: Taking a snapshot and terminating the instance eliminates compute charges entirely between test runs (paying only for snapshot storage), and restoring the snapshot recreates an instance with the exact same compute and memory configuration when needed.

explain: By creating a snapshot and terminating the DB instance, you effectively stop incurring costs for the running instance. When you need to run the tests again, you can restore the snapshot to create a new instance and resume testing. This approach allows you to save costs during the periods when the tests are not running.

q: A company stores data in Amazon S3. According to regulations, the data must not contain personally identifiable information (PII). The company recently discovered that S3 buckets have some objects that contain PII. The company needs to automatically detect PII in S3 buckets and to notify the company’s security team. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) notification to the security team.
o.w: GuardDuty is a threat-detection service for malicious activity and anomalous behavior; it does not scan S3 object contents for PII, so it cannot generate the needed PII findings.

o.t: Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to the security team.
o.w: Macie is purpose-built to discover and classify sensitive data such as PII in S3, and routing its SensitiveData finding type through EventBridge to SNS delivers an automatic notification to the security team.

o.t: Use Amazon Macie. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal event type from Macie findings and to send an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) notification to the security team.
o.w: SensitiveData:S3Object/Personal is a valid, more specific Macie finding type, but pairing it with Amazon SQS requires the security team to poll a queue rather than receive a pushed alert the way SNS provides.

o.t: Use Amazon GuardDuty. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter the CRITICAL event type from GuardDuty findings and to send an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification to the security team.
o.w: GuardDuty does not analyze object content for personally identifiable information, so filtering on its CRITICAL severity findings would not detect PII at all.

explain: Amazon Macie is a service designed for data discovery and classification. It can identify sensitive data, including personally identifiable information (PII). By creating an EventBridge rule to filter the SensitiveData event type, you can specifically target PII-related findings and notify the security team using Amazon SNS.

q: A company is designing a shared storage solution for a gaming application that is hosted in the AWS Cloud. The company needs the ability to use SMB clients to access data. The solution must be fully managed. Which AWS solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. Attach the file system to the origin server. Connect the application server to the file system.
o.w: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed file system that natively supports the SMB protocol, making it directly compatible with SMB clients for shared gaming application storage.

o.t: Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Assign an IAM role to the application to grant access to the S3 bucket. Mount the S3 bucket to the application server.
o.w: S3 is an object store accessed via HTTP APIs, not natively mountable by SMB clients, so it doesn't meet the SMB-access requirement without extra gateway components.

o.t: Create an AWS DataSync task that shares the data as a mountable file system. Mount the file system to the application server.
o.w: AWS DataSync is a data transfer service for moving data between storage systems; it does not itself expose data as a persistent, SMB-mountable shared file system for an application.

o.t: Create an Amazon EC2 Windows instance. Install and configure a Windows file share role on the instance. Connect the application server to the file share.
o.w: Installing a Windows file share role on an EC2 instance requires the company to manage, patch, and scale the server itself, which fails the fully managed requirement.

explain:
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed file storage service that is compatible with the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol, making it suitable for use with SMB clients, including Windows-based systems.
With Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, you can create a file system that can be mounted on application servers, providing shared storage for the gaming application.
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server handles the management aspects such as server provisioning, maintenance, and backups, making it a fully managed solution.

q: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones. The EC2 instances are in private subnets. A solutions architect implements an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) and specifies the EC2 instances as the target group. However, the internet traffic is not reaching the EC2 instances. How should the solutions architect reconfigure the architecture to resolve this issue?

o.t: Update the route tables for the EC2 instances’ subnets to send 0.0.0.0/0 traffic through the internet gateway route. Add a rule to the EC2 instances’ security groups to allow outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0.
o.w: Modifying route tables and security groups for outbound internet access doesn't address the issue, since the ALB itself needs to be reachable from the internet and route to the targets; outbound rules on the instances aren't the problem.

o.t: Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer. Configure a NAT gateway in a public subnet to allow internet traffic.
o.w: Swapping to a Network Load Balancer doesn't fix the ALB's subnet placement issue, and a NAT gateway handles outbound instance traffic, not inbound load balancer traffic.

o.t: Create public subnets in each Availability Zone. Associate the public subnets with the ALB. Update the route tables for the public subnets with a route to the private subnets.
o.w: An internet-facing ALB requires public subnets for its own nodes in each Availability Zone; placing the ALB's subnets as public while keeping the EC2 instances in private subnets, with routes between them, lets the ALB receive internet traffic and forward it to the private targets.

o.t: Move the EC2 instances to public subnets. Add a rule to the EC2 instances’ security groups to allow outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0.
o.w: Moving the EC2 instances to public subnets exposes them directly to the internet unnecessarily, since the ALB, not the instances, is what needs public subnet placement.

explain: This option involves creating public subnets for the ALB, allowing it to receive internet traffic. The EC2 instances can remain in private subnets. This approach follows the best practice of using public subnets for internet-facing components like ALBs.

q: A solutions architect is designing the storage architecture for a new web application used for storing and viewing engineering drawings. All application components will be deployed on the AWS infrastructure. The application design must support caching to minimize the amount of time that users wait for the engineering drawings to load. The application must be able to store petabytes of data. Which combination of storage and caching should the solutions architect use?

o.t: Amazon S3 with Amazon CloudFront
o.w: S3 scales to store petabytes of data durably, and CloudFront caches that content at edge locations close to users, minimizing the time it takes for engineering drawings to load.

o.t: Amazon S3 Glacier with Amazon ElastiCache
o.w: S3 Glacier is designed for archival data with retrieval delays measured in minutes to hours, which is incompatible with a requirement to minimize user-facing load times.

o.t: AWS Storage Gateway with Amazon ElastiCache
o.w: Storage Gateway is meant for hybrid on-premises-to-cloud storage integration, not as the primary petabyte-scale storage backend for a cloud-native web application.

o.t: Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes with Amazon CloudFront
o.w: EBS volumes are block storage tied to a single EC2 instance and are not designed to scale to petabytes or serve many users efficiently; CloudFront cannot use an EBS volume as an origin.

explain:
It is suitable for storing petabytes of data and is designed to provide low-latency access.
Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network (CDN) service that securely delivers data, videos, applications, and APIs to customers globally with low latency and high transfer speeds. By integrating CloudFront with S3, you can distribute the engineering drawings to edge locations worldwide, reducing the latency for users and improving load times.

q: A company is experiencing sudden increases in demand. The company needs to provision large Amazon EC2 instances from an Amazon Machine Image (AMI). The instances will run in an Auto Scaling group. The company needs a solution that provides minimum initialization latency to meet the demand. Which solution meets these requirements?

o.t: Use the aws ec2 register-image command to create an AMI from a snapshot. Use AWS Step Functions to replace the AMI in the Auto Scaling group.
o.w: Registering an AMI from a snapshot does not by itself reduce the time new volumes take to initialize from that snapshot; Step Functions only orchestrates the AMI swap and doesn't address the underlying latency.

o.t: Enable AMI creation and define lifecycle rules in Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (Amazon DLM). Create an AWS Lambda function that modifies the AMI in the Auto Scaling group.
o.w: DLM automates snapshot lifecycle policies such as creation and retention, not fast initialization of new EBS volumes from snapshots, so it doesn't address the initialization latency problem.

o.t: Enable Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) fast snapshot restore on a snapshot. Provision an AMI by using the snapshot. Replace the AMI in the Auto Scaling group with the new AMI.
o.w: Enabling EBS fast snapshot restore pre-warms the snapshot so that EBS volumes created from it, including when a new AMI is launched, achieve full performance immediately, eliminating lazy-loading latency during instance initialization.

o.t: Use Amazon EventBridge to invoke AWS Backup lifecycle policies that provision AMIs. Configure Auto Scaling group capacity limits as an event source in EventBridge.
o.w: AWS Backup lifecycle policies manage scheduled backups and retention; they don't change how quickly a new EBS volume initializes from a snapshot, so this does not reduce initialization latency.

explain:
Amazon EBS Fast Snapshot Restore: Enabling fast snapshot restore allows you to provision Amazon EBS volumes based on snapshots with faster performance. This is particularly useful when creating AMIs from snapshots, as it reduces the time it takes to create EBS volumes from those snapshots.

Minimum Initialization Latency: Fast snapshot restore helps in minimizing initialization latency as it provides a way to quickly create EBS volumes from snapshots.

Provisioning AMI from Snapshot: You can create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from an Amazon EBS snapshot. This allows you to capture a point-in-time snapshot of the file system, and then use that snapshot to create new instances.

q: A company recently migrated to AWS and wants to implement a solution to protect the traffic that flows in and out of the production VPC. The company had an inspection server in its on-premises data center. The inspection server performed specific operations such as traffic flow inspection and traffic filtering. The company wants to have the same functionalities in the AWS Cloud. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Use AWS Network Firewall to create the required rules for traffic inspection and traffic filtering for the production VPC.
o.w: AWS Network Firewall is a managed, stateful network firewall for VPCs that supports custom rules for traffic inspection and filtering, directly replacing the functionality of the on-premises inspection appliance.

o.t: Use AWS Firewall Manager to create the required rules for traffic inspection and traffic filtering for the production VPC.
o.w: AWS Firewall Manager centrally manages firewall rules, such as WAF and Network Firewall policies, across accounts; it is a management and orchestration layer, not itself a traffic inspection or filtering engine.

o.t: Use Traffic Mirroring to mirror traffic from the production VPC for traffic inspection and filtering.
o.w: Traffic Mirroring copies network traffic for out-of-band analysis or monitoring tools; it does not actively filter or block traffic in-line, so it can't replace an inspection-and-filtering appliance.

o.t: Use Amazon GuardDuty for traffic inspection and traffic filtering in the production VPC.
o.w: GuardDuty is a threat-detection service that analyzes logs and network flow metadata for malicious activity; it does not perform in-line traffic inspection or filtering of VPC traffic.

explain: AWS Network Firewall is a managed firewall service that provides filtering for both inbound and outbound network traffic. It allows you to create rules for traffic inspection and filtering, which can help protect your production VPC

q: A company hosts a three-tier web application that includes a PostgreSQL database. The database stores the metadata from documents. The company searches the metadata for key terms to retrieve documents that the company reviews in a report each month. The documents are stored in Amazon S3. The documents are usually written only once, but they are updated frequently. The reporting process takes a few hours with the use of relational queries. The reporting process must not prevent any document modifications or the addition of new documents. A solutions architect needs to implement a solution to speed up the reporting process. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of change to the application code?

o.t: Set up a new Amazon DynamoDB table to store the documents. Use a fixed write capacity to support new document entries. Automatically scale the read capacity to support the reports.
o.w: Moving to DynamoDB would require rewriting the relational queries used for reporting and redesigning the document-write model, which is a large code change, not the least.

o.t: Set up a new Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster that includes an Aurora Replica. Issue queries to the Aurora Replica to generate the reports.
o.w: Adding an Aurora PostgreSQL Replica lets the existing relational report queries run unchanged against the replica, offloading the multi-hour reporting workload from the primary without blocking writes, and requires minimal code change since Aurora is PostgreSQL-compatible.

o.t: Set up a new Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Configure the reporting module to query the secondary RDS node so that the reporting module does not affect the primary node.
o.w: Standard RDS Multi-AZ secondary nodes are passive failover standbys, not readable for offloading report queries in the classic Multi-AZ (non-Aurora) configuration, so this doesn't achieve the goal.

o.t: Set up a new Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) cluster that includes a read replica. Scale the read replica to generate the reports.
o.w: Migrating to DocumentDB, a different MongoDB-compatible database, would require rewriting all the existing SQL-based reporting and application logic, far more change than switching to a compatible Aurora replica.

explain: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL DB cluster that includes an Aurora Replica. Issue queries to the Aurora Replica to generate the reports) is the best option for speeding up the reporting process for a three-tier web application that includes a PostgreSQL database storing metadata from documents, while not impacting document modifications or additions, with the least amount of change to the application code.

q: A company is designing a containerized application that will use Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). The application needs to access a shared file system that is highly durable and can recover data to another AWS Region with a recovery point objective (RPO) of 8 hours. The file system needs to provide a mount target m each Availability Zone within a Region. A solutions architect wants to use AWS Backup to manage the replication to another Region. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with a Multi-AZ deployment
o.w: FSx for Windows File Server targets SMB-based Windows workloads and is not the natural fit for ECS Linux containers, and its cross-Region backup copy is not the simplest path to an 8-hour RPO for this use case.

o.t: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with a Multi-AZ deployment
o.w: FSx for NetApp ONTAP provides advanced features beyond what's required and is a more complex and costly option when a simpler, fully managed EFS solution already meets the Multi-AZ mount-target and RPO needs.

o.t: Amazon FSx for OpenZFS
o.w: FSx for OpenZFS does not provide a mount target in every Availability Zone within a Region the same way EFS does, nor does it integrate as simply with AWS Backup for the described cross-Region RPO.

o.t: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) with the Standard storage class
o.w: EFS Standard automatically provides a mount target in each Availability Zone within a Region, is highly durable, and AWS Backup can be configured to copy EFS backups to another Region to meet an 8-hour RPO.

q: A company is planning to migrate a TCP-based application into the company's VPC. The application is publicly accessible on a nonstandard TCP port through a hardware appliance in the company's data center. This public endpoint can process up to 3 million requests per second with low latency. The company requires the same level of performance for the new public endpoint in AWS. What should a solutions architect recommend to meet this requirement?

o.t: Deploy an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Configure the ALB to be publicly accessible over the TCP port that the application requires.
o.w: An ALB operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and is not designed for arbitrary TCP traffic on a nonstandard port, nor can it match the millions-of-requests-per-second throughput of a Layer 4 load balancer.

o.t: Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution that listens on the TCP port that the application requires. Use an Application Load Balancer as the origin.
o.w: CloudFront is an HTTP/HTTPS-oriented CDN; it does not natively listen on arbitrary nonstandard TCP ports, so it doesn't meet the requirement to handle raw TCP at this scale.

o.t: Deploy a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Configure the NLB to be publicly accessible over the TCP port that the application requires.
o.w: A Network Load Balancer operates at the TCP connection level (Layer 4), can be configured for any TCP port, and is built to handle millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency, matching the on-premises appliance's performance.

o.t: Deploy an Amazon API Gateway API that is configured with the TCP port that the application requires. Configure AWS Lambda functions with provisioned concurrency to process the requests.
o.w: API Gateway with Lambda is designed for HTTP/REST APIs, not generic TCP traffic on a nonstandard port, and would not sustain 3 million requests per second at the same low latency as a Layer 4 load balancer.

explain:
Network Load Balancer (NLB): It operates at the connection level (Layer 4) and is well-suited for TCP traffic. It can handle millions of requests per second with minimal latency.
NLB allows you to configure the listener for the specific TCP port that the application requires, ensuring compatibility with the nonstandard TCP port used by the application.

q: A media company uses an Amazon CloudFront distribution to deliver content over the internet. The company wants only premium customers to have access to the media streams and file content. The company stores all content in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company also delivers content on demand to customers for a specific purpose, such as movie rentals or music downloads. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Generate and provide CloudFront signed URLs to premium customers.
o.w: CloudFront signed URLs let the company generate time-limited, policy-controlled links that only premium customers receive, restricting access to specific pieces of on-demand content such as a single movie rental or download.

o.t: Generate and activate field-level encryption to block non-premium customers.
o.w: Field-level encryption protects specific sensitive form-field data in transit to the origin; it is not a mechanism for restricting which customers can view streaming or downloadable content.

o.t: Use origin access control (OAC) to limit the access of non-premium customers.
o.w: Origin access control restricts direct access to the S3 origin so that only CloudFront can fetch objects; it controls CloudFront-to-S3 access, not which end users are allowed to view the content through CloudFront.

o.t: Generate and provide S3 signed cookies to premium customers.
o.w: Amazon S3 does not issue signed cookies; signed cookies are a CloudFront feature, and cookies are generally better suited to granting access to multiple files at once rather than restricting single on-demand items.

explain: This solution involves generating signed URLs for the content, which allows access only to those who have the appropriate permissions. Signed URLs can be time-limited, and you can define custom policies specifying who can access the content and for how long.

q: A company collects 10 GB of telemetry data daily from various machines. The company stores the data in an Amazon S3 bucket in a source data account. The company has hired several consulting agencies to use this data for analysis. Each agency needs read access to the data for its analysts. The company must share the data from the source data account by choosing a solution that maximizes security and operational efficiency. Which solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Set up an IAM user for each analyst in the source data account. Grant each user access to the S3 bucket.
o.w: Creating individual IAM users for every analyst at every agency inside the source account is high operational overhead to manage and does not scale well as agencies or analysts change.

o.t: Configure cross-account access for the S3 bucket to the accounts that the agencies own.
o.w: Cross-account access via an S3 bucket policy lets each agency's own AWS account authenticate and read the data directly, without creating or managing external users in the source account, maximizing both security and operational efficiency.

o.t: Make the S3 bucket public for a limited time. Inform only the agencies.
o.w: Making the bucket public exposes the data to anyone on the internet, not just the intended agencies, which is the opposite of maximizing security.

o.t: Configure S3 global tables to replicate data for each agency.
o.w: Global tables are a DynamoDB replication feature, not an S3 capability; S3 has no mechanism by this name for sharing data this way.

explain: By configuring cross-account access, you can grant permissions to specific AWS accounts (owned by the consulting agencies) to access the S3 bucket. This allows you to share the data securely with the agencies without making the data public or creating additional IAM users in the source data account.

q: A company uses Amazon API Gateway to run a private gateway with two REST APIs in the same VPC. The BuyStock RESTful web service calls the CheckFunds RESTful web service to ensure that enough funds are available before a stock can be purchased. The company has noticed in the VPC flow logs that the BuyStock RESTful web service calls the CheckFunds RESTful web service over the internet instead of through the VPC. A solutions architect must implement a solution so that the APIs communicate through the VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the code?

o.t: Add an X-API-Key header in the HTTP header for authorization.
o.w: An X-API-Key header only adds authorization at the application layer; it doesn't change the network path, so the calls would still traverse the internet.

o.t: Use a gateway endpoint.
o.w: A gateway endpoint (a VPC endpoint type) is available only for S3 and DynamoDB, not for API Gateway, so it cannot be used to privately route traffic to the CheckFunds REST API.

o.t: Add an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue between the two REST APIs.
o.w: Inserting an SQS queue between the services requires redesigning the synchronous call into an asynchronous messaging pattern, which is a significant code change, not the fewest changes.

o.t: Use an interface endpoint.
o.w: An interface VPC endpoint, powered by AWS PrivateLink, for API Gateway lets BuyStock call CheckFunds over private connectivity within the VPC, keeping the existing HTTP call pattern with minimal code changes.

explain: Interface Endpoint (VPC Endpoint for API Gateway): An interface endpoint allows private connectivity to API Gateway within your VPC. By creating a VPC endpoint for API Gateway, you can ensure that the communication between the BuyStock and CheckFunds RESTful web services stays within the VPC, eliminating the need for traffic to go over the internet.

q: A company has an on-premises MySQL database that handles transactional data. The company is migrating the database to the AWS Cloud. The migrated database must maintain compatibility with the company's applications that use the database. The migrated database also must scale automatically during periods of increased demand. Which migration solution will meet these requirements?

o.t: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the database to Amazon Aurora. Turn on Aurora Auto Scaling.
o.w: DMS migrates the data while Aurora, which is MySQL-compatible, preserves compatibility with existing application code, and Aurora Auto Scaling automatically adds or removes Aurora Replicas to handle increased demand.

o.t: Use native MySQL tools to migrate the database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. Configure elastic storage scaling.
o.w: Standard Amazon RDS for MySQL supports storage auto-scaling but does not auto-scale compute or read capacity the way Aurora Auto Scaling with replicas does, making it a weaker fit for automatic scaling during demand spikes.

o.t: Migrate the database to Amazon Redshift by using the mysqldump utility. Turn on Auto Scaling for the Amazon Redshift cluster.
o.w: Amazon Redshift is a columnar data warehouse for analytics, not a drop-in replacement for a transactional MySQL OLTP database, so it would break application compatibility.

o.t: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB. Configure an Auto Scaling policy.
o.w: DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value and document database with a completely different data model and API than MySQL, so migrating to it would break compatibility with the existing MySQL-based applications.

explain:
AWS DMS is a fully managed service that helps you migrate databases to AWS easily and securely. It supports homogeneous and heterogeneous database migrations.
Amazon Aurora is a fully managed relational database service that is compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL. It provides high performance and availability with compatibility for MySQL, making it a seamless choice for migrating MySQL databases.

q: A company has multiple AWS accounts for development work. Some staff consistently use oversized Amazon EC2 instances, which causes the company to exceed the yearly budget for the development accounts. The company wants to centrally restrict the creation of AWS resources in these accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

o.t: Use AWS Organizations to organize the accounts into organizational units (OUs). Define and attach a service control policy (SCP) to control the usage of EC2 instance types.
o.w: Grouping accounts into OUs and attaching an SCP lets the company centrally restrict which EC2 instance types can be launched across all accounts in the OU with a single declarative policy and no code to write.

o.t: Develop AWS Systems Manager templates that use an approved EC2 creation process. Use the approved Systems Manager templates to provision EC2 instances.
o.w: Building custom Systems Manager templates for an approved EC2 creation process requires ongoing development and doesn't actually prevent staff from launching instances outside that process, so it does not centrally restrict resource creation.

o.t: Set up AWS Service Catalog products for the staff to create the allowed EC2 instance types. Ensure that staff can deploy EC2 instances only by using the Service Catalog products.
o.w: Building and maintaining Service Catalog products requires significant setup and governance effort and doesn't inherently prevent users with broader IAM permissions from still launching unapproved instance types directly.

o.t: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes an AWS Lambda function when an EC2 instance is created. Stop disallowed EC2 instance types.
o.w: Building a custom EventBridge and Lambda detection-and-remediation pipeline requires custom code to write and maintain, considerably more development effort than attaching a declarative SCP.

explain:
AWS Organizations allows you to consolidate multiple AWS accounts into an organization that you create and centrally manage.
Organizational Units (OUs) can be used to group accounts based on different criteria, such as development, production, etc.
Service Control Policies (SCPs) are used to set fine-grained permissions on AWS accounts within an organization.
By defining an SCP and attaching it to the OUs containing the development accounts, you can restrict the EC2 instance types that can be launched.

q: A company has a serverless website with millions of objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company uses the S3 bucket as the origin for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The company did not set encryption on the S3 bucket before the objects were loaded. A solutions architect needs to enable encryption for all existing objects and for all objects that are added to the S3 bucket in the future. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of effort?

o.t: Create a new encryption key by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). Change the settings on the S3 bucket to use server-side encryption with AWS KMS managed encryption keys (SSE-KMS). Turn on versioning for the S3 bucket.
o.w: Enabling default SSE-KMS encryption only applies to new objects going forward; it does not retroactively encrypt the millions of objects that were already uploaded unencrypted.

o.t: Navigate to Amazon S3 in the AWS Management Console. Browse the S3 bucket’s objects. Sort by the encryption field. Select each unencrypted object. Use the Modify button to apply default encryption settings to every unencrypted object in the S3 bucket.
o.w: Manually selecting and modifying millions of individual objects through the console does not scale and would take enormous manual effort, failing the least-effort requirement.

o.t: Turn on the default encryption settings for the S3 bucket. Use the S3 Inventory feature to create a .csv file that lists the unencrypted objects. Run an S3 Batch Operations job that uses the copy command to encrypt those objects.
o.w: Turning on default encryption covers all future uploads, while using S3 Inventory to list unencrypted objects and then running an S3 Batch Operations copy job to encrypt them in bulk efficiently handles the millions of existing objects with minimal manual effort.

o.t: Create a new S3 bucket. Turn on the default encryption settings for the new S3 bucket. Download all existing objects to temporary local storage. Upload the objects to the new S3 bucket.
o.w: Creating a new bucket and manually downloading and re-uploading millions of objects is slow, costly in data transfer, and far more effort than an in-place Batch Operations job.

explain: This option utilizes the S3 Inventory feature to generate a list of unencrypted objects in the S3 bucket. It then leverages S3 Batch Operations to perform a copy operation, allowing the encryption of the objects during the copy process. This approach is efficient and does not require downloading and re-uploading all existing objects.

q: A company's website handles millions of requests each day, and the number of requests continues to increase. A solutions architect needs to improve the response time of the web application. The solutions architect determines that the application needs to decrease latency when retrieving product details from the Amazon DynamoDB table. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?

o.t: Set up Amazon DynamoDB Streams on the table, and have AWS Lambda read from the table and populate Amazon ElastiCache. Route all read requests through ElastiCache.
o.w: Building a custom DynamoDB Streams, Lambda, and ElastiCache pipeline requires writing and maintaining custom caching logic, significantly more operational overhead than a managed caching layer purpose-built for DynamoDB.

o.t: Set up Amazon ElastiCache for Redis between the DynamoDB table and the web application. Route all read requests through Redis.
o.w: Standing up and managing a separate ElastiCache for Redis cluster requires provisioning, patching, and manually writing cache-invalidation logic in the application, more operational overhead than a purpose-built DynamoDB cache.

o.t: Set up Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached between the DynamoDB table and the web application. Route all read requests through Memcached.
o.w: ElastiCache for Memcached likewise requires the team to manage a separate cluster and write custom cache population and invalidation code, adding operational burden compared to a managed, DynamoDB-integrated cache.

o.t: Set up a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster. Route all read requests through DAX.
o.w: DAX is a fully managed, DynamoDB-specific in-memory cache that plugs in with minimal code changes and automatically caches frequently read items, cutting response times with the least operational overhead.

explain: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, highly available, and in-memory cache for DynamoDB. It is designed to improve the response time of read-intensive DynamoDB workloads by caching frequently accessed data. Using DAX helps reduce the read latency as it retrieves data from an in-memory cache instead of the DynamoDB table.

q: A financial company hosts a web application on AWS. The application uses an Amazon API Gateway Regional API endpoint to give users the ability to retrieve current stock prices. The company’s security team has noticed an increase in the number of API requests. The security team is concerned that HTTP flood attacks might take the application offline. A solutions architect must design a solution to protect the application from this type of attack. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

o.t: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with Lambda@Edge in front of the API Gateway Regional API endpoint. Create an AWS Lambda function to block requests from IP addresses that exceed the predefined rate.
o.w: Building a custom CloudFront and Lambda@Edge rate-limiting solution requires writing and maintaining custom logic to track and block IPs, far more operational overhead than a managed WAF rule.

o.t: Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to monitor the Count metric and alert the security team when the predefined rate is reached.
o.w: Monitoring the Count metric and manually alerting the security team only provides visibility, not automated protection; it does not actually block or throttle the flood of malicious requests.

o.t: Create a Regional AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule. Associate the web ACL with the API Gateway stage.
o.w: An AWS WAF rate-based rule automatically tracks request rates per IP and blocks addresses that exceed the threshold, and it can be directly associated with the API Gateway stage, giving managed, low-overhead flood protection.

o.t: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API Gateway Regional API endpoint with a maximum TTL of 24 hours.
o.w: Fronting the API with CloudFront and a long cache TTL doesn't stop malicious flood traffic targeting dynamic, per-request stock price data, since such requests generally bypass or invalidate caching.

explain: Rate-based Rule with AWS WAF: AWS WAF provides protection against various web application attacks, including HTTP flood attacks. By using a rate-based rule, you can set thresholds for the number of requests from a client IP within a specified time period. This helps in detecting and mitigating HTTP flood attacks effectively.

q: A company's infrastructure consists of hundreds of Amazon EC2 instances that use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage. A solutions architect must ensure that every EC2 instance can be recovered after a disaster. What should the solutions architect do to meet this requirement with the LEAST amount of effort?

o.t: Take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance. Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk to set the environment based on the EC2 template and attach the EBS storage.
o.w: Manually snapshotting every instance and recreating environments with Elastic Beanstalk requires custom orchestration and isn't designed as a centralized backup and restore mechanism for an existing EC2 fleet.

o.t: Use AWS Backup to set up a backup plan for the entire group of EC2 instances. Use the AWS Backup API or the AWS CLI to speed up the restore process for multiple EC2 instances.
o.w: AWS Backup centrally manages and automates backup plans across the entire fleet of EC2 instances, and its API or CLI supports efficient bulk restores, meeting the recovery requirement with minimal manual setup.

o.t: Take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance. Create an AWS CloudFormation template to launch new EC2 instances from the EBS storage.
o.w: Manually snapshotting every instance and then building a custom CloudFormation template for restoration is a manual, hard-to-scale process across hundreds of instances compared to a centralized backup service.

o.t: Create an AWS Lambda function to take a snapshot of the EBS storage that is attached to each EC2 instance and copy the Amazon Machine Images (AMIs). Create another Lambda function to perform the restores with the copied AMIs and attach the EBS storage.
o.w: Writing and maintaining custom Lambda functions to handle snapshotting, AMI copying, and restoration for hundreds of instances is considerably more development and operational effort than using a managed backup service.

explain:
AWS Backup: AWS Backup is a fully managed backup service that centralizes and automates the backup of data across AWS services. 
Backup Plan: You can set up a backup plan in AWS Backup to create and manage backups of the entire group of EC2 instances. 
AWS Backup provides a streamlined process for restoring data. You can use the AWS Backup console, API, or AWS CLI to initiate the restore process for multiple EC2 instances.

q: A company wants to implement a disaster recovery plan for its primary on-premises file storage volume. The file storage volume is mounted from an Internet Small Computer Systems Interface (iSCSI) device on a local storage server. The file storage volume holds hundreds of terabytes (TB) of data. The company wants to ensure that end users retain immediate access to all file types from the on-premises systems without experiencing latency. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST amount of change to the company's existing infrastructure?

o.t: Provision an Amazon S3 File Gateway as a virtual machine (VM) that is hosted on premises. Set the local cache to 10 TB. Modify existing applications to access the files through the NFS protocol. To recover from a disaster, provision an Amazon EC2 instance and mount the S3 bucket that contains the files.
o.w: An S3 File Gateway only caches a subset of data locally, far less than the hundreds of terabytes involved, and requires switching the on-premises application to NFS from iSCSI, both reintroducing latency for uncached files and more change than necessary.

o.t: Provision an AWS Storage Gateway tape gateway. Use a data backup solution to back up all existing data to a virtual tape library. Configure the data backup solution to run nightly after the initial backup is complete. To recover from a disaster, provision an Amazon EC2 instance and restore the data to an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume from the volumes in the virtual tape library.
o.w: A tape gateway with nightly backups to a virtual tape library does not provide immediate access to all file types at all, since tape-based backup is for archival and restore, not live access, and this changes the backup method significantly.

o.t: Provision an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway stored volume with the same amount of disk space as the existing file storage volume. Mount the Volume Gateway stored volume to the existing file server by using iSCSI, and copy all files to the storage volume. Configure scheduled snapshots of the storage volume. To recover from a disaster, restore a snapshot to an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume and attach the EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance.
o.w: A stored volume keeps a full local copy of all data, unlike a cached volume, giving on-premises users the same zero-latency access they have today while asynchronously backing up snapshots to AWS for disaster recovery, with minimal change since it's mounted via the same iSCSI protocol.

o.t: Provision an AWS Storage Gateway Volume Gateway cached volume. Set the local cache to 10 TB. Mount the Volume Gateway cached volume to the existing file server by using iSCSI, and copy all files to the storage volume. Configure scheduled snapshots of the storage volume. To recover from a disaster, restore a snapshot to an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume and attach the EBS volume to an Amazon EC2 instance.
o.w: A cached volume keeps only frequently used data locally and fetches less-used data from S3 on demand, introducing latency for file types not in the cache and failing the immediate-access-to-all-files requirement.

explain: Explanation: A cached volume only keeps the most frequently accessed data locally — anything not in cache has to be fetched from S3 first, adding latency, so it fails the "immediate access to all file types" requirement. A stored volume keeps the entire dataset on-premises (with async backup to S3), giving true zero-latency access to every file.

q: An ecommerce company runs a PostgreSQL database on premises. The database stores data by using high IOPS Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) block storage. The daily peak I/O transactions per second do not exceed 15,000 IOPS. The company wants to migrate the database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and provision disk IOPS performance independent of disk storage capacity. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

o.t: Configure the General Purpose SSD (gp2) EBS volume storage type and provision 15,000 IOPS.
o.w: gp2 IOPS scale with the provisioned storage size rather than being independently provisioned, so the company cannot simply provision 15,000 IOPS on gp2 without buying far more storage than needed, making it not cost-effective here.

o.t: Configure the General Purpose SSD (gp3) EBS volume storage type and provision 15,000 IOPS.
o.w: gp3 lets you provision IOPS independently of the volume's storage size, so the company can get exactly 15,000 IOPS without over-provisioning storage, at a lower price point than io1.
